title: Saltpeter Cave at Carter Caves
summary: Saltpeter Cave in Carter Caves State Resort Park in Carter County was mined for potassium nitrate during the War of 1812 to make gunpowder.
bodyMarkdown:
Saltpeter Cave (15Cr99) lies inside Carter Caves State Resort Park near Olive Hill in Carter County. It has also been called Swingle's Cave and Swindell's Cave. In the early 1800s miners dug its dry, nitrate-rich dirt to make saltpeter, the main ingredient of black gunpowder.

## A War of 1812 niter mine

The cave's [National Register nomination](https://npgallery.nps.gov/GetAsset/d20b40c8-b5b8-4dfb-8d2c-bfd8cc0c4835) explains why the work mattered. During the war, British blockades cut off imported gunpowder, so Americans turned to the limestone caves of the Southeast. Kentucky became the leading producer, with hundreds of saltpeter mines. The form names Saltpeter Cave, Mammoth Cave and Great Saltpeter Cave as the most productive cave mines of the period.

The link to the war rests partly on local tradition. Plummer family records and local accounts say the cave's niter went into powder fired at the Battle of New Orleans in 1815. The nomination reports that archival searches, including DuPont's records at the Hagley Museum and the National Archives, found nothing to prove or disprove that story.

It still judges the case for War of 1812 operation strong. [Saltpeter Cave](https://grokipedia.com/page/saltpeter_cave) also presents the 1812 use as local tradition.

## What the miners left

Miners loaded cave earth into wooden vats, ran water through it, and boiled the resulting "niter beer" with a potash solution until crystals formed. Spent dirt was piled to the side. More than 620 cubic meters of these spoil piles still narrow the first room of the cave.

The vat counts differ within the nomination. One page says at least 17 of 25 identified vats sit in the first room. Another says more than 25 leaching vats are present. Fewer than half a dozen are V-shaped, and the form reads those as later, smaller mining episodes.

Archaeological work in 1992, reported in a University of Kentucky master's thesis by Duncan (1993), found intact wooden vat sides, bottoms and troughs just below the surface.

## Output and price

Kentucky supplied 301,937 pounds of saltpeter to the war effort in 1812, according to figures quoted in the nomination. Its conservative estimate for this cave alone is 25,800 to 43,000 pounds. The nomination gives two prewar prices: 12 to 15 cents a pound in one passage and 17 cents in 1810 in another. Both passages put the wartime price at 75 cents to a dollar. Local legend says digging stopped when the war ended and prices fell.

## Kentucky today

Saltpeter Cave was listed on the National Register in 2001. Its measured length is 3.05 kilometres (1.90 miles). It is a winter hibernaculum for the endangered Indiana bat, so tours run only in summer, from Memorial Day to Labor Day.

[Carter Caves State Resort Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Caves_State_Resort_Park) notes that mining history is a major part of the tour. The nearby falls have their own story, [Carter Caves' Cascade Falls](/stories/carter-caves-cascade-falls/).
